new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is final: nouns are most often stressed on the last syllable, adjectives/adverbs likewise carry lexical stress (contrastive pairs exist), derivational suffixes (-ey, -ın, -ıj, -i, oblique plural -an) are inherently stressed and take the stress, while unstressed inflectional suffixes (plural -i, case -ı, -ê, person-number endings, enclitic copula) do not shift stress off the stem-final syllable. Verbs: stress on the last syllable of the (past or present) stem; the subjunctive/future/imperative prefix bı-, negative nê-, prohibitive me- and negative copula niy- are always stressed and override stem stress; imperatives and subjunctives without bı- stress the first syllable. Because a lexical subclass (feminine di-/trisyllabic nouns in unstressed -i/-ı) is penult-stressed and minimal contrasts exist, Todd classes stress as phonemic 'in strictly phonological terms', though 'largely predictable' and of low functional load (endnote 11: 'Stress, however, does not carry a very significant burden in the distinction of lexical items').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; no mention of secondary stress anywhere in the grammar.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) feminine nouns of two or three syllables ending in unstressed /i/ or /ı/ are stressed on the penult (all nouns in unstressed -ı are feminine); (b) unstressed inflectional suffixes leave stress on the original syllable even when it becomes penultimate; (c) inherently stressed suffixes (definite plural oblique -an, derivational -ey, -ın, -ıj, -i) attract stress; (d) stressed verbal prefixes bı-, nê-, me- supersede stem-final stress; imperative/subjunctive stress the first syllable; (e) personal names are made vocative by stressing the first syllable; (f) stress is contrastive in some adjective/adverb pairs.
new_statements.identity_note: Todd describes the speech of a single speaker ('A') from a village about 45 km north of Siverek (Qirwar tribe), i.e. Southern Zazaki / Siverek Dimili, with occasional contrasts to Çermik speakers and to Mann-Hadank (1932) on Siverek and Kor.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: the catalog's fixed: final syllable code and Todd (2002/2008) both put default stress on the final syllable (of the noun; of the verb stem). The one tension is typological labelling: Todd states that stress 'is not completely predictable' and 'in strictly phonological terms it is phonemic' because a subclass of feminine nouns ending in unstressed -i/-ı is penult-stressed and a few adjective/adverb pairs contrast by stress, whereas a bare fixed: final syllable code implies full predictability. Todd himself calls stress 'largely predictable' and of low functional load (endnote 11), so the catalog record stands with these exceptions noted.

Rayîra bîne de derb bi tonê vengî ya yeno meydan. Ziwanê fekkî de derbo sentaktîk mîyanê cumle de bi tonê vengî ya yeno saz kerdene. tone.translation: Stress arises in three ways. One of them: a syllable is pronounced more forcefully and clearly than the other syllables. Stress mostly arises in this way. In another way, stress arises through the pitch (tone) of the voice. In the spoken language, syntactic stress within the sentence is produced by the pitch of the voice. [...] In Zazaki, as in Kurmanji, stress is mostly on the last syllable (Taş 2013: 31).

tone.translation: The falling and rising of the voice vibrations during speech is called tone. [...] In some languages tone is very important. For example, monosyllabic languages known as isolating languages, such as Chinese, Thai, Tibetan and Vietnamese, are known as tone languages. [...] For example, when we want to load the sentence 'Ti senîn mi kenê xo vîr ra.' with meanings such as anger, surprise, reproach or question, we intone the sentence in different ways.
